topic: The Library of Babel, Jorge Luis Borges

slides.title: Imagine a library that holds every possible book.

slides.kicker: A library made of endless rooms.
slides.body:
In 1941, the Argentine writer Jorge Luis Borges published a short story called "The Library of Babel".

In it, the universe is a vast maze of six-sided rooms, lined with shelves of books, stretching in every direction.

slides.kicker: Every book follows the same rules.
slides.body: Every possible combination of these symbols fills a book somewhere. So every text ever written is there. And every text never written.

When people realised the library held every book, Borges writes, they were wildly happy.

Somewhere on those shelves was the answer to every question. Even a book that explained and justified their own life.

For every sentence that made sense, there were miles of gibberish.

The true catalogue of the library was there. So were thousands of false ones. Nobody could tell which was which.

Jonathan Basile, a literature graduate, put a version of the library online. Type any sentence, and it shows you the page where it already exists.

But open a page at random, and you rarely find more than seven English letters in a row.

slides.lead: Having every answer is worth nothing if you can't tell which one is true.
slides.accent: Meaning comes from choosing, not collecting.

slides.line: Save this for the next time you're drowning in information.

caption:
In 1941, Borges imagined a library holding every possible book. Every answer, every truth, every lie. And it drove its readers to despair.

In 2015, someone actually built it online. It's still useless, and still fascinating. 📚

What would you search for first?
